paragraphs.text: Discourses Against the Jews, by Our Father among the Saints, John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople. Discourse One. 1. Today I wanted to give you the rest of the subject I discussed with you recently, and to show more clearly how God is incomprehensible. Last Sunday we gave those many long discourses on this subject, and brought forward as witnesses Isaiah, David and Paul. The first cried out, “Who shall declare his generation?” The second gave thanks to God for his incomprehensibility, saying, “I will confess to you, for you are fearfully made wonderful; wonderful are your works,” and again, “Your knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is mighty, I cannot attain to it.” Paul did not peer into the investigation of God's very essence, but only into his providence. Or rather, he grasped only a small part of that providence, the part God displayed in the calling of the Gentiles. Yet as though he were looking at a vast and fathomless sea, he cried out: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out!” The proof from these witnesses was sufficient. But I was not content with the prophets, and I did not stop at the apostles. I went up to heaven and showed you the choir of angels saying, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men.” You heard the seraphim too, struck with awe and crying out with trembling, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory.” I added the cherubim as well, crying out, “Blessed be his glory [?]” … [text garbled] … [?] against those who Judaize and fast with the Jews.

… discourses against the Anomoeans can be given at another time too, and no harm would come from putting them off. But those who are sick with the Jewish disease must be healed now, when the feasts of the Jews are near and at the doors. If we do not heal them, I fear that some, from ill-timed habit and great ignorance, may take part in the Jews' lawlessness, and then our words on these matters will be in vain. If they hear nothing today and fast with the Jews, we will be applying the remedy uselessly, after the sin has been committed. That is why I hasten to get in first. Doctors do the same: they deal first with the most pressing and acute diseases. And in any case this contest is closely related to the earlier one. The impieties of the Anomoeans and of the Jews are related, so our present contests are related to the earlier ones. The charge the Jews made is the same charge the Anomoeans make. What did the Jews charge? That he called God his own Father, making himself equal to God. The Anomoeans charge this too. Or rather, they do not merely charge it: they erase the saying along with its meaning, if not with their hand, then with their mind. 2. Do not be surprised that I called the Jews wretched. They truly are wretched and miserable, for so many good things came into their hands from heaven, and they eagerly thrust them away and cast them off. The Sun of righteousness rose for them first, and they thrust away its ray and sit in darkness. We, who were brought up in darkness, drew the light to ourselves and were freed from the gloom of error. They were branches of the holy root, but they were broken off. We had no share in the root, and we bore the fruit of godliness. They read the prophets from their earliest youth and crucified the one the prophets foretold. We had not heard the divine oracles, and we worshiped the one who was foretold. They are wretched because they repelled the good things sent to them, while others seized those things and drew them to themselves. They were called to adoption as sons and fell away to kinship with dogs. We were dogs, and by the grace of God we were able to put off our former irrationality and rise to the honor of sons. How is this clear? “It is not good,” he says, “to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs.” Christ said this to the Canaanite woman, calling the Jews children and the Gentiles dogs. But see how afterward the order was reversed: they became dogs, and we became children. Paul says of them, “Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the mutilation; for we are the circumcision.” Do you see how those who were once children became dogs? Do you want to learn how we, who were once dogs, became children? “But as many as received him,” he says, “to them he gave power to become children of God.” Nothing is more wretched than those who run against their own salvation at every turn. When they ought to have kept the law, they trampled on it. Now that the law has ceased, they contend for keeping it. What could be more pitiable than people who provoke God not only by breaking the law but also by keeping it? That is why he says, “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart, you [?]” … in mind and in purpose. [Notes:] Ibid.: some manuscripts read “But do not be surprised” [?] … in the margin [?] … “the Sun of righteousness rose for them first” [?]; and most manuscripts and Morel read “of that root.” Savile [?]. “For they fell away” [?]. Three manuscripts read “to Christ.”

… the rabble of [?] women, they drag the whole theater and the people from the stage into the synagogue, for there is no difference between a theater and a synagogue. I know that some condemn what I said as bold, because I said there is no difference between a theater and a synagogue. But I condemn their boldness if they do not think so. If I were declaring this on my own authority, condemn me. But if I am speaking the words of the prophet, accept the verdict. 3. I know that many respect the Jews and think their present way of life is venerable. That is why I hasten to tear this deadly notion up by the roots. I said that the synagogue is no better than a theater, and I bring testimony from a prophet; the Jews are not more trustworthy than the prophets. What then does the prophet say? “You had a harlot's brow; you became shameless before all.” Where a harlot has set herself up, the place is a brothel. Or rather, the synagogue is not only a brothel and a theater; it is also a den of robbers and a lair of wild beasts. “Your house has become to me a hyena's den,” he says. Not simply the den of a beast, but of an unclean beast. And again: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance.” When God forsakes a place, what hope of salvation is left? When God forsakes it, that place becomes a dwelling of demons. But surely they will say that they too worship God. God forbid that I should say so! No Jew worships God. Who says this? The Son of God. “If you knew my Father,” he says, “you would know me also; but you neither know me nor know my Father.” What testimony could I bring that is more trustworthy than this? If, then, they do not know the Father, crucified the Son, and rejected the help of the Spirit, who would not boldly declare that the place is a lair of demons? God is not worshiped there, God forbid! That place is from now on a place of idolatry. And yet some people still frequent those places as if they were venerable. I am not saying this from guesswork; I have learned it by experience. Three days ago (believe me, I am not lying) I saw a respectable free woman, modest and a believer, being forced by a foul and senseless man who passed for a Christian (I would not call anyone who dares such things a sincere Christian) to go into the Hebrews' place and swear an oath there about matters in dispute between them. The woman came up to me, called for help, and begged me to stop this lawless violence, for it was not lawful for her, as one who shared in the divine mysteries, to go into that place. Kindled with zeal and on fire, I rose up and did not let her be dragged any further into that lawlessness; I snatched her away from this unjust abduction. Then I asked the man who was dragging her whether he was a Christian, and he admitted it. I came down hard on him, charging him with senselessness and the utmost folly. I told him he was no better than a donkey if he claimed to worship Christ and yet dragged someone to the dens of the Jews, who crucified him. And I gave him a long talk. First I taught him from the divine Gospels that it is not lawful to swear at all, or to force others to take oaths. Then … [Notes:] Three manuscripts read “presides.” [?] “to declare … the demonic [?].” Below: “run to the places.” [?] Five manuscripts read “and to stop the lawless violence.” Others read “that one; but I snatched.” Ibid.: others read “and to the one dragging.” Others read “to you,” and shortly after “fearful” instead of [?].

… is. It is a lodging not merely of robbers and hucksters but of demons. And not only the synagogues are such places, but the very souls of the Jews as well; I will try to show this toward the end of the discourse. So I urge you to remember this discourse above all. We are not speaking now for display or applause, but for the healing of your souls. For what excuse is left to us when, with so many physicians at hand, there are some

… the apostles were twelve, and they drew in the whole world. The greater part of this city is Christian, and yet some are still sick with Judaism. What defense could we who are healthy offer? Those who are sick deserve blame, of course. But we are not free from accusation either, since we neglect them in their sickness. If they were receiving much zeal from us, they could not possibly remain in that weakness. That is why I am saying this now, ahead of time, so that each of you may draw in your brother. Even if you have to use compulsion, or force, or insults, or argument, do everything to rescue him from the devil's snare and free him from fellowship with the killers of Christ. Tell me: if you saw someone in the marketplace being led away after being condemned in court, and you had the power to snatch him from the executioner's hands, would you not do everything to free him from being led away? Now you see your brother being dragged unjustly and impiously toward the pit of destruction, not by an executioner but by the devil. Would you not even bring yourself to give him advice and so rescue him from that lawlessness? What pardon could you expect? “But he is stronger and more powerful than you.” Bring him to me. I will sooner choose to lay down my head than let him set foot on the sacred threshold if he obstinately persists with them [?]. What do you have in common with the free woman, with the Jerusalem above? You chose the one below; be a slave with her. For she too is in slavery with her children, as the Apostle says. You fast with the Jews? Then take off your shoes with the Jews too, walk barefoot in the marketplace, and share in their indecency and laughter. But you would not choose that; you are ashamed and you blush. So you are ashamed to share their outward appearance, yet you are not ashamed to share their impiety? [text garbled] What pardon will you have, when you are a Christian [?]? Believe me, I would sooner lay down my head than overlook anyone I see sick with such things. But if it happens through ignorance, God will surely grant pardon. Let each of you consider this too, and not think the matter a side issue. What does the deacon keep crying out at the mysteries? [?] See how he entrusts to you the scrutiny of your brothers? Do the same with these people. When you find someone Judaizing, hold him back and make it known, so that you do not share in it yourself [?]. In the armies on campaign, if a soldier is found siding with the barbarians and taking the Persians' part, he is not the only one in danger. So is everyone who knew about him and did not report him to the general. Since you too are Christ's army, [examine] carefully … [Notes:] Others read “is the place of that one.” [?] “for this reason we say what we say.” Shortly after, some read thus: “a word for you when.” [?] “Christians.” Others read “to snatch” [?] … [?] “advice” … “you endure.” [?] “declaring such things about them, as to dare to speak of their … impiety” [?].

… [?] the saints, and insulting them. Executioners who hold the bodies of martyrs and abuse them no less: will they be revered for that? Would that not be the height of irrationality? If bodies held wrongfully not only fail to sanctify those who hold them but make them more accursed, then much more can writings read with unbelief never benefit those who read them. In fact, the very fact that they hold the books with such a disposition shows them to be more impious. They would not deserve such great accusation if they did not have the prophets; they would not be so unclean and profane if they did not read the books. As it is, they are deprived of all pardon, because they have the heralds of the truth and yet set themselves against those heralds and against the truth with a hostile mind. So they are all the more profane and accursed for this reason: they have the prophets and treat them with hostility. Therefore I urge you to flee their gatherings and leap away from them. They do no small harm to the weaker brothers and give the Jews no small occasion for arrogance. When they see you, who worship the Christ they crucified, pursuing their ways and revering them, how can they not think that they have done everything perfectly well and that our ways are worthless? After all, you who champion and serve our ways are running to those who destroy them. “For if anyone sees you who have knowledge,” he says, “reclining at table in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, since he is weak, be emboldened to eat food offered to idols?” And I say: if anyone sees you who have knowledge going into a synagogue and watching the trumpets, will not his conscience, since he is weak, be emboldened to admire the Jewish ways? Someone who falls pays the penalty not only for his own fall; he is also punished for tripping up others. Likewise someone who stands is not only crowned for his own virtue; he is also admired because he leads others to the same zeal. So flee their gatherings and their places. Let no one revere the synagogue because of the books. Rather, let him hate it and turn away from it for this very reason: they hold the saints in contempt, they disbelieve their words, and they accuse them of the utmost impiety. 6. So that you may learn that the books do not sanctify the place, but rather the disposition of those who gather there makes it profane, I will tell you an ancient story. Ptolemy Philadelphus gathered books from everywhere. He learned that the Jews too had writings that taught wisdom about God and about the best way of life. So he sent for men from Judea, had the writings translated by them, and deposited them in the temple of Serapis, for the man was a pagan. To this day the translated books of the prophets remain there. What then? Will the temple of Serapis be holy because of the books? God forbid! The books have their own holiness, but they do not pass it on to the place, because of the defilement of those who gather there. The same must be said of the synagogue. Even if no idol stands there, … [Notes:] Some manuscripts have “flee and run past their.” Others read “for their own.” [?] “Flee then,” but [?]. Others read “Sarapis,” and similarly. In the edition of Athanasius [?] often “Serapis” and “Serapion.” On the story of Ptolemy and the translation of the Scriptures, still preserved in his time [?] … “among these.”

… Wild beasts often give up even their lives and disregard their own safety to protect their young. But these people, under no compulsion, slaughtered their own children with their own hands, to serve avenging demons, the enemies of our life. What should astonish us first: their impiety, or their cruelty and inhumanity? That they sacrificed their sons, or that they sacrificed them to demons? And in licentiousness, did they not outdo even the most lustful of beasts? Hear what the prophet says about their lack of restraint: “They became [?] horses; each neighed after his neighbor's wife.” He did not say “each desired his neighbor's wife.” He used the cry of brute animals, most expressively, to show the madness their licentiousness produced in them. What else do you want me to mention? Their robberies, their greed, their betrayals of the poor, their thefts, their sharp dealing? A whole day would not be enough to recount them. [?] “But their feasts are something venerable and great” [?]. Yet they made even these feasts unclean. Hear the prophets, or rather hear God, and see how strongly he turns away from them: “I hate, I have rejected your feasts.” God hates them, and you take part in them? And he did not say this feast or that one, but all of them together. Do you want to see that he also hates the worship with drum, lyre, harp and other instruments? “Take away from me the sound of your songs,” he says, “and I will not listen to the music of your instruments.” God says, “Take it away from me,” and you run to hear the trumpets? But are not these sacrifices and offerings an abomination? “If you bring me fine flour, it is in vain; incense is an abomination to me.” Incense is an abomination, and [?] not an abomination? And it was an abomination even then, before they committed the crowning evil and killed their own Master, before the cross, before they killed Christ. Is it not much more so now? Yet what is more fragrant than incense? But God judges offerings by looking not at the nature of the gifts but at the disposition of those who bring them. He looked upon Abel, and then upon his gifts. He saw Cain, and then turned away from his sacrifices. “For upon Cain,” it says, “and upon his sacrifices he did not look.” Noah offered God sacrifices of sheep, calves and birds, and Scripture says, “The Lord smelled a pleasing odor,” that is, he accepted what was offered. For God has no nostrils; the divine is incorporeal. What rose up from that altar was the reek and smoke of burning bodies, and nothing smells worse than such a reek. But God calls the reek and the smoke a pleasing odor and calls incense an abomination, so that you may learn that he accepts or rejects sacrifices by looking at the disposition of those who offer them; for the disposition of those who brought the incense was full of foulness. Do you want to learn that he also turns away from the temple, along with the sacrifices, the instruments, the feasts and the incense, because of those who went into it? He showed this above all by his deeds: at one time he handed it over to barbarian hands, and later he destroyed it completely. But even before its destruction he cries out through the prophet and says, “Do not trust in lying words, for they will not profit you [?] …” [Note:] Some manuscripts read “made unclean” [with a different verb]; Morel and others read [?].

…your [?], and with all your soul." From this it is clear that demons do not heal. And if, with God's permission, they should ever manage some healing, as men do, the permission is given to test you. It is not that God does not know; it is so that you may learn not to put up with the demons even when they heal. And why do I speak of bodily healing? If someone threatens you with hell to make you deny Christ, do not give in. If someone promises you a kingdom to make you desert the only-begotten Son of God, turn away and hate him. Become a disciple of Paul, and imitate the words which that blessed and noble soul cried out: "For I am convinced," he says, "that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Neither angels, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor any other creature separates him from the love of Christ, and does bodily healing draw you away? What pardon could we obtain? For Christ ought to be more fearful to us than hell itself, and more desirable than the kingdom. Even if we fall ill, it is better to stay in our sickness than to fall into impiety in order to be rid of the illness. Even if a demon heals, it does more harm than good. It helps the body, which will certainly die a little later and is going to rot, but it harms the immortal soul. Kidnappers often hold out sweets and cakes and knucklebones and other such things to little children, and by luring them in this way they rob them of their freedom and even of their very life. In just the same way the demons promise healing for a limb and sink the whole salvation of the soul. But let us not put up with it, beloved. Let us by every means seek to be freed from impiety. Could not Job have listened to his wife, blasphemed against God, and been rid of the calamity that lay upon him? "Speak some word against the Lord," she says, "and die." But he chose rather to suffer and waste away and bear that unbearable blow than to blaspheme and be freed from the evils upon him. You too must imitate him. Even if the demon promises you countless ways out of the evils that weigh on you, do not be persuaded and do not give in, just as the righteous man was not persuaded by his wife. Choose rather to endure the illness than to lose your faith and the salvation of your soul. For when God often lets you fall into illness, it is not because he is abandoning you, but because he wants to make you more glorious. So remain steadfast, so that you too may hear: "Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown righteous…

[?] There would be more to say than this, but so as not to spoil your memory of what has been said, I will end my discourse here with the words of Moses: "I call heaven and earth to witness against you" that if any of you, whether present or absent, goes off to watch the Trumpets, or runs to the synagogue, or goes up to the shrine of Matrona, or shares in a fast, or takes part in sabbaths, or keeps any other Jewish custom, small or great, I am innocent of the blood of you all. On the day of our Lord Jesus Christ these words will stand beside both me and you. If you obey them, they will give you great confidence. But if [?] … [?] that has taken place.

Of St John Chrysostom. To those who keep the fast of the Jews, and to the Jews themselves. Delivered five days before their fast, after another discourse had already been given. Second Discourse.

1. The lawless and unclean fast of the Jews is now at the doors. Do not be surprised that I have called it unclean, though it is a fast. Whatever is done against the will of God, whether it be a sacrifice or a fast, is the most abominable thing of all. Their lawless fast, then, is coming upon us in five days. But I got ahead of it and gave you my exhortation ten days or more beforehand, so that you might make your brothers safe. Let no one condemn the discourse as untimely because we delivered it so many days in advance. When a fever or some other illness is expected, people take the lead and protect the body that is about to be attacked with many treatments, hurrying to snatch it from the dangers to come before it feels their onset. In the same way, since we see a most grievous disease about to approach, we gave warning well in advance and long beforehand, so that the correction might take place before the evil is felt. That is why I did not give my exhortation right at the days themselves. I did not want the shortness of the time to hinder you in hunting down your brothers. With the room that so many days afford, you can track down and win back those who suffer from this disease in complete freedom. People who are holding weddings and preparing costly banquets do the same thing. They do not wait for the day itself, but talk with fishermen and fowlers long beforehand, so that the shortness of time does not get in the way of preparing the table. Since we too were going to set before you a table against the senselessness of the Jews, we spoke to you, the fishermen, in advance, so that you might net the weaker of your brothers and bring them to hear our words. Those of you who have made your catch and hold it safely within the nets, keep drawing the nets tighter with the word of exhortation. Those of you who have not yet secured this fine prey have time enough, these five days, to succeed in the hunt. Let us spread out the nets of teaching, then, and stand around them in a circle like hunting dogs, driving them together from every side into the laws of the Church. And, if you agree, let us bring against them the blessed Paul, as a most excellent huntsman, crying out and saying: "Look, I, Paul, tell you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no benefit to you." Many wild and savage animals hiding under a bush leap out in fear when they hear the huntsman's voice. Driven by the force of that voice, and often pushed along by the shouting even against their will, they fall right into the traps. So too your brothers, who are hiding in Judaism as in a bush, if [?] … (Savile conjectures that we should read "that correction might take place." Shortly after: "to cause trouble idly and in vain?") But indeed also

why did Paul put his own name here, instead of simply saying, "Look, I tell you"? He wanted to remind them of the zeal he had shown for Judaism. "If I were from the Gentiles," he is saying, "and ignorant of Jewish things, someone might perhaps have said that I am throwing circumcision out of the doctrines of the Church because I never took part in that way of life and do not know its force." That is why he put his own name, recalling to their memory what he had done on behalf of the law. It is almost as if he were saying: "I do this not out of hostility to circumcision, but because I know the truth. I, Paul, say this. I am that Paul who was circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel, a Hebrew of Hebrews, of the tribe of Benjamin, as to the law a Pharisee, as to zeal a persecutor of the Church, the one who went into houses, dragged off men and women, and handed them over to prison." All of this could persuade even the most senseless that "it is not from any hostility, nor from ignorance of Jewish things, but from knowledge of the surpassing truth of Christ that I have laid down this law." "And I testify again," he says, "to every man who accepts circumcision, that he is obliged to keep the whole law." Why did he not say "I command," or "I enjoin," or "I say," but "I testify"? He wanted this word to remind us of the coming judgment, for where there are witnesses, there is a court and a verdict. So he frightens the hearer by reminding him of the royal throne. He shows that these words will be witnesses against him on that day, when each person will give an account of what he has done, and of what he has said and heard. The Galatians heard these things then. Let those who now suffer from the Galatians' disease hear them too. Even if they are not present, let them hear through you Paul crying out and saying: "I testify to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obliged to keep the whole law." Do not tell me that circumcision is only one commandment. That one commandment lays the entire yoke of the law upon you. When you bring yourself under the lordship of the law through one part of it, you must obey its other commands as well. And if you do not fulfil them, you must certainly be punished and bring the curse upon yourself. When a sparrow falls into a snare, even if only its foot is held, the whole rest of its body is caught too. In the same way, whoever keeps one commandment of the law, whether circumcision or fasting, has by that one commandment handed over all his own freedom to the law. He will not be able to escape so long as he is willing to obey it even in part. We do not say these things to accuse the law. God forbid! We say them because we want to show the surpassing wealth of Christ's grace. The law is not opposed to Christ. How could it be, when he gave it and it leads us to him like a tutor? But we are forced to say all this because of the untimely contentiousness of those who use it wrongly. They are the ones who insult the law, for when it commands them to leave it once for all and come to Christ, they cling to it again. I too acknowledge that the law has been of the greatest benefit to our nature, and I would never deny it. But by clinging to it out of season, you do not let the greatness of its benefit be seen. Just as the greatest praise a tutor could have would be [?] … no longer caught in charges of impiety, and toward

…being dragged off into licentiousness. For prostitutes and effeminate men and the whole troupe from the theater usually flock there. [?] Why do I speak of the fornications that take place? Are you not afraid that your wife will come back from there carrying a demon? Did you not hear in the previous discourse, when our argument clearly showed that demons dwell both in the very souls of the Jews and in the places where they gather? Tell me, then: how do you dare to dance with demons and then come back to the assembly of the apostles? How can you go off and share with those who shed the blood of Christ, and then come and share in the holy table and partake of the precious blood, without shuddering? Do you not shudder? Are you not afraid to commit such lawlessness? Have you no reverence for the table itself? I have said these things to you. You must say them to those men, and they must say them to their wives. Build one another up, each the other. If the one who suffers from this disease is a catechumen, let him be barred from the porch. If he is a baptized believer who has been initiated, let him be driven from the holy table. Not all sins call for exhortation and counsel. Some are of the kind that is corrected by a quick and very sharp cut. With wounds, the milder ones yield to gentler remedies, while those that are festering and incurable and spreading to the rest of the body need the edge of the knife and the fire. [?] Amen.

Against Those Who Fast the First Pascha. Third Discourse.

1. Once again a necessary and urgent need has broken the thread of what we were saying before. It draws our discourse to itself and leads us away today from our contests with the heretics. We were preparing to speak to your love again about the glory of the Only-begotten. But the untimely contentiousness of those who want to fast the first Pascha compels us to devote our whole teaching today to their healing. The good shepherd does not only drive off the wolves. He also tends the sick sheep with all care. What is gained if the flock escapes the jaws of the wild beasts but is devoured by disease? In the same way, a good general does not only beat back the siege engines. Before that, he reconciles the city that is quarreling with itself, knowing that a victory outside will do no good so long as civil wars remain within. To learn that nothing destroys like strife and contentiousness, hear what Christ says: "A kingdom divided against itself will not stand." Yet what is more powerful than a kingdom? It has revenues of money, weapons, walls, fortifications, a great number of soldiers, horses, and countless other things that give it great strength. And yet all this power is dissolved when it quarrels with itself. Nothing produces weakness so surely as contentiousness and strife, just as nothing [?] … (A Regius manuscript reads: "the flocks, but within by the…")

[?] … would become, even small things, when they receive the care they need. So the first thing we say to them is this: nothing is worse than contentiousness and fighting and tearing the Church apart. The robbers did not dare to tear that tunic, yet they cut it into many pieces. Are the other heresies not enough, that we must also cut ourselves to pieces? Do you not hear Paul saying, "But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another"? Tell me: you are walking outside the flock, and you are not afraid of the lion prowling around outside? "For your enemy," he says, "prowls around like a lion, roaring and looking for someone to seize." See the wisdom of the shepherd. He did not let the lion be inside among the sheep, so that he would not terrify the flock. Nor did he drive him far away outside, so that fear of the beast would gather everyone inside. Do you have no respect for your father? Then fear the enemy. If you cut yourself off from the flock, he will certainly receive you. Christ could have driven him away even from outside. But in order to make you sober and watchful and quick to keep running to your mother for refuge, he let him roar outside. Then those within, hearing his voice, draw closer together and take refuge with one another. Loving mothers do the same. When their children cry, they often threaten to throw them into the jaws of the wolves, not in order to throw them, but to stop their fussing. Christ did all things for this purpose, that we might be at peace and bound to one another.

2. This is why Paul too, though he had many serious charges to bring against the Corinthians, charged them with nothing before this. He could have charged them with fornication, with arrogance, with going to outside law courts, with banqueting in idol temples, and with women not covering their heads while men did. On top of all this, he could have charged them with contempt for the poor, with the arrogance their gifts produced in them, and with their views on the resurrection of the body. Along with all these, he could also rebuke them for their contentiousness and dissension with one another. He passed over everything else and corrected that first. If I do not seem to be troubling you, I will show from Paul's own words that, although he had all those charges to bring, he corrected none of them before this. That they were committing fornication, hear what he says: "It is actually reported that there is fornication among you." That they were puffed up and arrogant: "Some have become puffed up, as though I were not coming to you." That they were again going to court outside: "When any of you has a matter against another, does he dare to go to law before the unbelievers?" That they were eating food sacrificed to idols: "You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons." And about women not covering their heads while men did the opposite, hear how he rebukes them: "Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, and every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head." And that they despised the poor, he made this clear too, saying, "One goes hungry and another gets drunk," and again, "Or … the church of God

[?] … was I unacquainted with life under the law and with the punishment laid down for those who break the law? [?: "his name be called upon"; "concerning Jerusalem"] "A Hebrew of Hebrews, as to the law a Pharisee, as to zeal a persecutor of the Church." "But whatever gains I had, these I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ"; that is, I left them once and for all. "Become as I am, for I too was as you are." And why do I speak of myself? Three hundred fathers or more gathered in the land of the Bithynians and laid down this law. Do you dishonor them all? It must be one of two things. Either you condemn them for folly, as if they did not know accurately, or for cowardice, as if they knew but pretended and betrayed the truth. When you do not keep to what they decreed, one of these conclusions must follow. Everything that happened shows that they displayed great wisdom and courage at that time. Their wisdom is shown by the faith they set forth then. It stopped the mouths of the heretics and, like an unbreakable wall, beat back all their schemes. Their courage is shown by the persecution that had just ended, the war waged against the Churches. Like champions who have set up countless trophies and received many wounds, the leaders of the Churches came back from everywhere at that time bearing the marks of Christ. They had many punishments to recount which they had endured for their confession. Some could tell of the mines and the hardships they suffered there. Others could tell of the confiscation of all their property, others of hunger, others of constant beatings. Some could show their sides scraped raw, others their backs broken, others their eyes gouged out, others some other part of the body cut off for Christ's sake. The whole council was assembled from these athletes. Along with the faith, they also decreed that this feast should be celebrated together and in harmony. These men did not betray the faith in such terribly hard times. Were they going to pretend over the observance of days? Consider what you are doing when you condemn so many fathers, so brave and so wise. If the Pharisee lost all the good he had by condemning the tax collector, what pardon will you have, what defense, when you rise up against so many teachers who are friends of God, and do it unjustly and with great folly? Do you not hear Christ saying, "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am among them"? If Christ is among them where two or three are gathered, then much more was he present where three hundred and many more were gathered, and he shaped and decreed everything. You condemn not only them but also the whole world, which approved their decision. Or do you think the Jews are wiser than the fathers in every part of the earth? And this when they have fallen from their ancestral way of life and celebrate no feast at all? For they have no unleavened bread and no Pascha. Indeed, I hear many people say this too, that the Pascha goes with the unleavened bread. To see that they have no unleavened bread, hear the lawgiver saying: "You may not keep the Pascha in any of your cities which the Lord your God gives you, but only in the place which, if [?] …" (Reg.: "what will be")

…freeing him from every observance of days. For Pascha and Lent are not the same thing: Pascha is one thing and Lent another. Lent comes once a year, but Pascha three times a week, sometimes four, or rather as often as we wish. For Pascha is not a fast; it is the offering and the sacrifice that takes place at every assembly. To see that this is so, listen to Paul saying, "Christ, our Pascha, was sacrificed for us"; and, "As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death." So as often as you approach with a clean conscience, you celebrate Pascha, not when you fast but when you share in that Sacrifice. "For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death." And to proclaim the death is Pascha. For the offering made today, the one performed yesterday, and the one made every day is like the one made on that day of the Sabbath, and indeed the same. That one is no more solemn than this, and this no less precious than that. They are one and the same, equally awe-inspiring and saving. "Why then," someone says, "do we fast these forty days?" In the old days many approached the mysteries casually and just as it happened, especially at this season, when Christ handed them down. So the fathers, aware of the harm that came from approaching carelessly, met together and laid down forty days of fasting, prayers, hearing the Scriptures and assemblies. In these days all of us would be carefully purified through prayers, almsgiving, fasting, vigils, tears, confession and every other means, and so approach, as far as we are able, with a clean conscience. That they achieved something great by this concession, settling us into a habit of fasting, is clear from the following. If we spend the whole year crying out and preaching fasting, no one pays attention to what is said. But once the season of Lent arrives, even the most sluggish person rouses himself without anyone exhorting or advising him, taking his counsel and exhortation from the season itself. So if a Jew or a Greek asks you why you fast, do not say it is because of the Pascha or because of the cross, since that gives him a great handle against you. We do not fast because of the Pascha or because of the cross, but because of our sins, since we are about to approach the mysteries. The Pascha is no occasion for fasting or mourning, but for gladness and joy. For the cross took away sin. It became the cleansing of the world and the reconciliation of a long enmity. It opened the gates of heaven, made friends of those who were hated, led them back to heaven, seated our nature at the right hand of the throne, and has given us countless other blessings. So we ought not to mourn or be downcast, but to exult and rejoice over all these things. That is why Paul says, "Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." And again: "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners [?]" Patrologia Graeca XLVIII.

…"that we may not be kept back from the gifts of the Lord?" "Stand here," he says, "and we will refer it to God." Then, when he had referred it, he brought back a law that said, "If anyone is unclean because of a corpse, or is on a long journey, [?] …to your brother, and then come and offer your gift [?] …and cannot keep the Pascha in the first month, he shall keep it in the second." [?] What are you saying? If your brother has something [?]… So for the Jews the observance of the time is relaxed, so that the Pascha may be held in Jerusalem. And you, will you not put the concord of the Church ahead of the time? Just to be seen observing days, will you outrage the common mother of us all and tear the holy assembly apart? How could you deserve pardon when you choose to sin so greatly for nothing at all? And why speak of the Jews? Even if we wished it very much and tried hard, it is quite impossible for us to keep the very day on which he was crucified, as is clear from the following. Suppose the Jews were not transgressors, not ungrateful, not insensible, not lazy and contemptuous, and had not fallen away from their ancestral way of life, but kept it precisely even now. Even so, we could not hit upon the very day on which he was crucified and kept the Pascha by following them. How so? When he was crucified, it was the first day of Unleavened Bread and also the Day of Preparation, and these two cannot always coincide. Look: this present year the first day of Unleavened Bread falls on a Sunday, and we must fast the whole week. The passion is past, the cross and the resurrection have taken place, and we go on fasting. This has often happened: after the cross and after the resurrection, before the week was complete, the fast was still being kept. So there is no real observance of the time. Let us not be contentious, then, or say, "I have fasted at this time for so long, and am I to change now?" For that very reason, change! You have been cut off from the Church for so long, so come back at last to your mother. No one says, "I have stayed at enmity for so long that I am ashamed to be reconciled now." The shameful thing is not changing for the better but persisting in untimely contentiousness. This is what destroyed the Jews too. Always seeking the old custom, they were swept away into impiety. And why do I speak of fasting and the observance of days? Paul went on keeping the law. He endured much sweat, made many journeys, bore many other hardships, and surpassed all his contemporaries in the strictness of that way of life. Yet after he had driven himself to the very height of that way of life, when he realized that he was doing everything to his ruin and harm, he changed at once. He did not say to himself, "What is this? Am I to forfeit so much zeal? Am I to lose so much labour?" On the contrary, for that very reason he changed all the more quickly, so as not to remain in the same loss. He thought nothing of the righteousness in the law in order to receive the righteousness that comes from faith, and he cries out, "Whatever was gain to me, I have counted as loss for Christ's sake." "If you are offering your gift," he says, "at the…" [Note:] So the Regius manuscript; [?] however has "despised."

Against the Jews [?]. [?] …I am not concerned about the time [?]… [since it seemed good to the fathers, though in different places,] [?] to come together and fix this day, it was right [?] for God, as we have shown, since [?] everywhere they honour concord above [?] … I have spent many words on this. But I am eager for one thing only: that we do everything in peace and harmony. While we and the whole people are fasting, and the priests are offering common supplications for the whole world, you must not stay at home getting drunk. Consider how this is the devil's work, and how the sins are not one, or two, or three, but many more. He cuts you off from the flock and leads you to condemn so many fathers. He throws you into contentiousness, pushes you toward the Jews, and makes you a stumbling block once again to your own people and to outsiders. How will we be able to accuse those who stay at home [?] when you run to them? And these are not the only sins. Great harm would also follow, since in those fasts you enjoy neither the Scriptures, nor the assemblies, nor the blessing, nor the common prayers. Instead you spend this whole time with a bad conscience, afraid and trembling that you will be caught, like some foreigner and alien, when you ought to do everything in common with the Church, with confidence, with pleasure, with gladness and with complete freedom. For the Church does not insist on exactness of dates either. But since from the beginning it seemed good to all the fathers, though they were divided…

[?] By the Same, Against the Jews, on the Trumpets of Their Pascha. Delivered at Antioch in the Great Church. Fourth Discourse.

1. Once again the wretched Jews, the most miserable of all people, are about to fast, and once again it is necessary to secure Christ's flock. Shepherds behave the same way. As long as no wild beast troubles them, they throw themselves down under an oak or a pine and play on their reed pipes, leaving the sheep to graze in complete freedom. But when they sense that wolves are making a raid, they quickly throw down the reed and take up the sling. Leaving the pipe, they arm themselves with clubs and stones, stand in front of the flock, and raise a great shout that carries far, and often they drive the beast away with their voice alone, before throwing a stone. So too with us. In the days before, we frolicked in the exposition of the Scriptures as if in a meadow and took up no combative discourse, since there was no one to trouble us. But today the Jews, more dangerous than any wolves, are about to surround our sheep, so we must box and fight, so that none of ours becomes the prey of the beast. And do not be surprised if, with that fast still ten or more days away, we are already arming ourselves from this moment and fencing in your souls. Industrious farmers act the same way: when they have a torrent nearby that sweeps away their fields, they do not [wait until] the… [Note:] [?] "delivered at Antioch in the Great [Church]" [?] Savile [?]. In the Morel editions, [?] "…by the same, against the Jews" [?].

…urging you to flee this accursed and lawless fast. Do not tell me that they fast. Show me instead whether they do it according to God's will. If they do not, their fast is more lawless than any drunkenness. We must not consider only what they do; we must also look for the reason behind what is done. What is done according to God's will, even if it seems bad, is the best thing of all. What is done against his will and does not please him, even if it is thought the best, is the worst and most lawless thing of all. If someone kills according to God's will, that killing is better than any kindness. But if someone spares and shows kindness against what pleases him, that sparing would be more unholy than any murder. For it is not the nature of things but the decrees of God that make the same things good or bad.

2. To learn that this is true, listen. Ahab once captured a king of the Syrians. Against God's will he saved him, let him sit beside him, and sent him away with great honour. Then a prophet came and said to his neighbour, "By the word of the Lord, strike me." And the man would not strike him. And he said to him, "Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord, look, you are going away from me, and the lion will strike you." And he went away from him, and the lion found him and struck him. And he finds another man and said, "Strike me." And the man struck him and wounded him, and he bound up his face. What could be more astonishing than this? The man who struck the prophet was saved, and the man who spared him was punished. This is so that you may learn that when God commands, we must not busy ourselves with the nature of what is done, but simply obey. So that the first man would not spare him out of reverence for the prophet, he did not just say, "Strike me," but, "By the word of the Lord." That is: God has commanded, so ask nothing further. It is a king who gives the law. Respect the dignity of the one who commands, and obey with all eagerness. But the man refused, and so he paid the ultimate penalty, and through what he suffered he warns those who come after to yield and obey in everything God commands. Then, when the second man had struck and wounded him, he bound his head with a bandage, hid his eyes, and made himself unrecognizable. Why did he do this? He was going to rebuke the king and pass sentence on him for sparing the king of the Syrians. Since the king was impious and always hostile to the prophets, the prophet feared that if the king saw him, he would drive him from his presence, and having driven him away would not accept correction. So he hid both his face and the account of the matter, so that by speaking he might prevail and get the king to agree to what he wanted. For when the king was passing by, he cried out [?]… but since they are punished for wickedness. So here too, pass judgment on what is done. If you see people fasting for God's sake, approve what is done. But if you see them doing it against God's will, turn away from them and hate them more than those who get drunk, run riot and carouse. In the case of this fast…

…we must look not only at the reason but also at the place and the time. But before turning to the Jews, I will gladly speak with our own members. They seem to be ranked with us, yet they keep the Jews' observances and have taken up the whole fight on their behalf. In this respect I see them as deserving greater condemnation than all the Jews. Not only the wise and intelligent would agree with us on this, but anyone with any share of reason and understanding. There is no need for clever arguments, elaborate proofs or long periods to show it. It is enough to ask a simple question and convict them by their answer. What then? I will ask each of those who suffer from this sickness: Are you a Christian? Then why are you so eager for the ways of the Jews? Are you a Jew? Then why do you trouble the Church? Does the Persian not think as the Persians do? Does the barbarian not follow barbarian ways? Does the one who lives in Roman territory not follow our way of life? Tell me: if someone living among us is caught holding their views, is he not punished at once, without a hearing or an inquiry, even if you have countless defences to offer? And if someone among them is found using Roman laws, will he not suffer the very same in turn? How then can you pass over to that lawless way of life and still expect to be saved? Is the difference between us and the Jews a small one? Is the dispute about trivial matters, so that you think the two are one and the same? Why do you mix what cannot be mixed? They crucified Christ, whom you worship. Do you see how great the difference is? How then can you, who say you worship the Crucified, run to those who killed him? Am I the one introducing this rule for the charges and this kind of accusation? Does Scripture not use this same approach against them? Listen to what Jeremiah says to those very people: "Go to Kedar and see; send to the islands of Kittim, and find out whether such things have happened: whether nations change their gods, though they are not gods. But you have changed your glory, from which you will gain nothing." He did not say, "You have changed your God" [?], but "your glory." What he means is this. Those people, he says, worship idols and serve demons, yet they are so committed to their error that they will not choose to leave those things and go over to the truth. But you, who worship the true God, have abandoned your ancestral piety and gone over to foreign ways. You have not shown as much commitment to the truth as they have to this error. That is why he says, "whether such things have happened, whether nations change their gods, though they are not gods. But you have changed your glory, from which you will gain nothing." He did not say, "You have changed your God," for God does not change, but, "You have changed your glory." You have not wronged me, he says; no harm has come to me. You have dishonoured yourselves. You have not diminished my glory but your own. Allow me, too, to say the same to our people, if indeed we should call "ours" those who think as the Jews do. Go to the synagogues and see whether the Jews have changed their fast, whether… [Notes:] Seven manuscripts have "to be" and "you mix." [?] "he did not say, 'You have changed your God,' but 'your glory'" [?] are missing. In some manuscripts [?] "they grew fat, they grew broad."

…[to consider] whether we should disregard the place and keep the time, or disregard the time and keep the place. What I mean is this. He commanded that the Pascha be held both in the first month and in Jerusalem: at a fixed time and in a fixed place. Let us suppose, then, that two people are keeping the Pascha. Let one violate the place but keep the time, and the other keep the place but violate the time. The one who keeps the time but violates the place holds it in the first month, somewhere far outside Jerusalem. The one who keeps the place but violates the time holds the Pascha in Jerusalem, not in the first month but in the second. Then let us see which of these two is blamed and which approved: the one who broke the time and held it in the place, or the one who left the place and kept the time. Suppose the one who broke the time in order to hold it inside the city turns out to deserve approval, while the one who kept the time but left the place turns out to deserve charges and accusation, as if he had acted impiously. Then it is plain that these people, too, are breaking the law by not holding it in the place, even if they say ten thousand times that they keep the time. How will this become clear? From Moses himself. When they kept the Pascha outside [?], some people came to Moses, it says, saying, "We are unclean because of a human corpse. Are we to be kept back from offering the gift of the Lord at its appointed time among the children of Israel?" And Moses said to them, "Stand here, and I will hear what the Lord will command concerning you." And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the children of Israel and say: Any man who becomes unclean because of a human corpse, or is on a long journey, whether among you or in your generations, shall keep the [Pascha] in the second month." What he means is this: whoever is abroad in the first month must not hold it outside the city, but in the second month, so that he can reach Jerusalem. Let him break the time so as not to lose the city. By this he shows that observing the place is more necessary than observing the time. What then could those who hold it outside the city say? When they break the more necessary rule, even their observance of the lesser one cannot defend them. So even if they appear ten thousand times over not to break the time, they commit the utmost lawlessness. And this is clear not only from here but also from the prophets. Those people in exile are shown neither offering sacrifice, nor singing a song in a foreign land, nor fasting any fast of this kind. So what pardon could these people have? Those in exile expected to recover their way of life, and still they remained obedient to the law and kept its commands, because this is what the law said. These people have no hope of recovering their former way of life (where can they show this from the prophets?), and even so they cannot bear to keep quiet. Yet even if they did expect to recover it, they ought still to imitate those holy men and not fast [?], and not do any such thing.

5. To see that those men did none of these things, listen… [Notes:] [?] "for where do they have," which comes to the same thing. Below, Savile and very many [?]… "not to fast" [?]… One [manuscript] has "all the feasts outside the…" (So [?].)

[?] could contribute anything great; nor, when they were abandoned, did that have power to make the earnest man worthless, or to diminish anything of the philosophy in his soul. These men, at any rate, who by their philosophy displayed on earth a way of life that rivalled the angels, performed none of these things: they offered no sacrifice, kept no feast, displayed no fast of this kind. Yet they so pleased God that they even overcame nature itself, and through what happened to them drew the whole world to the knowledge of God. For what could equal Daniel? And what could equal the three youths? They anticipated the greatest commandment in the Gospels, the sum of all good things, and displayed it already in their deeds. "Greater love than this," he says, "no one has, that a man lay down his life for his friends." But they laid down their lives for God. And they are wonderful not for this alone, but because they did it not for any reward either. That is why they said, "There is a God in heaven who is able to deliver us; and if not, be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods." The reward is enough for us, he means, that we die for God's sake. And they did these things and displayed this virtue while observing none of the customary rites.

6. "And why," someone says, "did God command these things, if he did not want them done? And if he wanted them done, why then did he destroy your city?" For, if he wanted them to remain, he ought to have done one of two things: either not to command that sacrifice be offered in one place, if he was going to scatter you over the whole world; or, if he wanted you to sacrifice only there, not to scatter you over the whole world and make inaccessible the one city in which alone the sacrifice had to be offered. What then? Does he contradict himself, someone says, commanding sacrifice in one place and then closing off that very place? Not at all; on the contrary, he is entirely consistent with himself. For he did not wish to give you sacrifices even at the beginning; and for this I bring forward the prophet himself as witness, who says: "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give heed to the law of your God, you people of Gomorrah." He is speaking not to the Sodomites and those who lived in Gomorrah, but to the Jews. He calls them this because by imitating their wickedness they drew upon themselves kinship with them. So too he calls them dogs and lust-crazed horses, not because they had changed into the nature of those creatures, but because they pursued the lewdness of these animals. "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord." Those in Sodom were never seen offering sacrifices; rather, the word is aimed at these people, calling them by the name of those others for the reason I have given. "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord. I am full of whole burnt offerings of rams, and the fat [?]"

[?] for the Jews, where it is not lawful to sacrifice, Jerusalem alone has become inaccessible, the one place where alone it was lawful to sacrifice? Would not the reason for that destruction be clear and evident even to the utterly foolish? For just as a builder who has laid foundations, raised walls, vaulted a roof, and bound that vault together into one middle stone undoes the whole bond of the building if he removes that stone, so too God, having made the city a kind of bond of worship, and then overturning it, destroyed the whole remaining edifice of that way of life.

7. So let the battle against the Jews rest for the moment. For today we have skirmished with them, saying only as much as was enough for the safety of our brothers, or rather much more. But it remains necessary to urge you who are present [?] to take great care of our members, so that you may not say: "What does it matter to me? Why should I meddle and busy myself?" Your Master died for us [?], and do you not even utter a word? What pardon will you have? What defense will you find? How, tell me, will you stand with boldness before the judgment seat of Christ, if you overlook the ruin of so many souls? If only it were possible for me to know those who run there! Then I would not have needed you, but would have made the swiftest correction myself [?]. When you must correct a brother, even if you have to give up your life, do not refuse; imitate your Master. Whether you have a servant or a wife, keep them at home with great firmness. If you do not allow them to go to the theater, much more must you do this in the case of the synagogue; for this transgression is greater than that one: what happens there is sin, but here it is impiety. We say this not so that you will let them go up to the theater (for that too is evil), but so that you will prevent this much more. Why, tell me, do you run to see men blowing trumpets in the synagogue of the God-fighting Jews? You ought to sit at home groaning and weeping for them, because they fight against God's command, because they have the devil dancing with them. For as I said before, what is done against God's will, even if it was once permitted, afterwards becomes a transgression and an occasion for countless punishments. The Jews once blew trumpets, when they had their sacrifices; but now they are not permitted to do this. Hear, then, why [?] the silver trumpets. Then, stating their use, he added: "And you shall blow on them at your whole burnt offerings [?] and at the sacrifices of your peace offerings." Where then is the [?]? Where is the ark? Where is the tabernacle, and the holy of holies? Where is the priest? Where are the cherubim of glory? Where is the golden censer? Where is the mercy seat? Where only [?]

[?] "that they may make much of the past days"; others, "much of the present days," etc. [?] "that you may take much [care] of our members": so the translator read it. A little later others [?] "what pardon will you have" [?]. Savile: "but so that both those and these much [?]" [?]. Others: "so that both that and this." AGAINST THE JEWS. Fifth Discourse.

1. Why has our gathering grown larger today? Surely you have come to demand the fulfilment of my promise, and you are here to receive the refined silver which I promised to pay out. For "the words of the Lord," it says, "are pure words, silver refined by fire, tested in the earth." Blessed be God, who has put in you so great a desire to hear spiritual teaching. Just as lovers of wine and drinkers rise each day and inquire and busy themselves about where there are drinking parties and banquets and dinners and revels and drunkenness and bowls and mixing bowls and cups, so you too rise each day and inquire where there is exhortation and counsel and encouragement and teaching and a discourse that tends to the glory of Christ. That is why we ourselves take up this subject more eagerly, and pay out what we promised with all good will. The battle against the Jews has reached its proper end: the trophy stands, the crown has been made ready for us, and we carried off the prize already in the former discourse. For our aim was to show that what they are doing now is a transgression and a violation of the law, a fight and a war of men against God; and this, with God's help, has been shown with complete precision. For even if they were going to recover their city, and return to their former way of life, and see the temple rising again (which will never happen), not even so would they have any defense for what they are doing now. For the three youths, and Daniel, and all the others who lived in the captivity, expected to recover their city, to see the soil of their homeland after seventy years, and to live under their former laws; and yet, though they had a clear and acknowledged promise, not even so did they dare, before the promise was fulfilled and they returned, to perform any of the legal observances which these people perform now. In this way you too will be able to stop the Jew's mouth. Ask him: "Why do you fast, when you do not have the city?" And if he says, "I expect to recover the city," say to him: "Then keep quiet until you recover it. For those saints too [?]"

[?] until you accept it, and do not think it trustworthy; but if you see him speaking the truth in all things, and this prediction too fulfilled, and [?] time bearing witness to the truth of what was foretold, do not be shameless any longer, nor contend against things clearer than the sun. Let us see, then, what else he foretold. [?] There came to him a woman with an alabaster jar of very costly ointment, and she poured out the oil. 4. What has been said was enough to prove that the temple will never be raised again. But since the truth is so abundantly supplied, I will leave the Gospels and turn to the prophets, whom they seem to believe most of all, and from them I will make it plain that they will never again recover either the city or the temple. And yet I was under no necessity to prove that it will not be raised, nor was this my task; it was theirs to show the opposite, that it will be raised. For I have the confirmation that time provides, bearing witness for me and fighting at my side; but they, who are defeated by the very outcome of events and have nothing to show in deeds of what they say, but boast simply and idly, are the ones who ought to supply this testimony. For what I say, I show to have come to pass through the facts themselves: both that the city fell, and that it has not risen again in so long a time; but what they say rests on their bare words. And they ought to show that the city will rise again, since we see proofs handled this way in the law courts too. For when people dispute with one another about anything, and one party furnishes written proofs of what he says, and then the other takes issue with what is said, it is the latter who is then compelled to produce witnesses or other evidence that things are not as the documents say, not the one who produces the documents. So now too the Jews ought to do the same, and bring before us a prophet who says that the city will surely rise again. For if the present captivity were going to have an end for you, the prophets would necessarily have foretold it; this is evident to anyone who has even glanced into the prophetic books. For it was an ancient custom among the Jews that the prophets foretold far in advance the evils or the good things that were going to befall them. For what reason, and why? Because of their great ingratitude and shamelessness. For they immediately forgot the God who had done them good, ascribed what happened to the demons, and credited the good things to them. At one time, having come out of Egypt, when the sea had been split and the other miracles had been done, they forgot the God who had done these things and attributed what happened to gods that are no gods, and said to Aaron, "Make us gods who will go before us." And to Jeremiah too they are seen saying: "The word which you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord we will not hear from you; but we will surely do every word that goes out of our mouth, to burn incense to the queen of heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, both we and our fathers, our kings and our rulers; and we were filled with bread, and were well off, and saw no evil. And since we [?] burning incense to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have all been diminished, and have perished by sword and by famine." So, in order that they might not credit any of what befell them to the idols, but believe that both punishments and benefits always came to them from God, the former because of their sins and the latter out of his love for humankind, the prophets foretold to them far in advance what was going to happen.
