[?] Others read "the presence, I am ashamed." Others read "of the storm," others "of the error."

…they sailed into the calm harbour, bringing not gold or silver or costly garments, but treasures no one can plunder: endurance, courage and love. Now they belong to Paul's choir. Even before their crowns, the expectation of those crowns gives them wings, and from now on they have escaped the uncertainty of the future. Why then would they need our words? For this very reason this subject is more welcome to them. As I said already, our praises will add nothing to their own glory. But they would take great pleasure in contests against the Jews, and they would listen most gladly of all to these words spoken for the glory of God. The martyrs hate the Jews above all, because they loved so intensely the one whom the Jews crucified. The Jews said, "His blood be upon us and upon our children"; the martyrs poured out their own blood for the one the Jews killed. So they would gladly listen to these words. 2. We have shown well enough that if the present servitude were going to end, the prophets would have foretold that too and would not have kept silent. We showed that every captivity came upon them with a prediction: the one in Egypt, the one in Babylon, the one under Antiochus Epiphanes. For each of these we showed from the divine Scriptures that both a time and a place had been announced in advance. But no prophet set a time for the present one. Daniel foretold that it would come, lay everything waste and overturn their polity, and how long after the return from Babylon it would happen. But neither he nor any other prophet revealed that it would have an end, or that these evils would stop anywhere. On the contrary, he foretold that this servitude would hold them until the end of the age. The long time that has passed since then bears witness to these words. To this day it has shown no trace and no beginning of a change for the better, even though they have often tried to rebuild the temple. Once, twice and three times, under Hadrian, Constantine and Julian, they made the attempt and were stopped: the first times by soldiers, later by fire bursting out of the foundations, which checked their ill-timed contentiousness. Now I would gladly ask them: Tell me, why is it that after spending so long a time in Egypt you recovered your own country, and after being carried off again to Babylon, [?] you came to Jerusalem? Again, after suffering such evils under Antiochus, you returned to your former state, and once more you recovered the sacrifices, the altar, the holy of holies, and everything with its former dignity. But now nothing of the kind has happened. A hundred years have passed, and twice, three and four times that many, and far more besides (for it is now the five hundredth year from then to our time). Yet nowhere do we see even a hint of such a change appearing. Instead their affairs have utterly collapsed, and not even in a dream do they show such… [?] "bearing," says [?], who printed "carrying out." [?] Others read "but that even twice." [?] "but has collapsed."

…[?] for what reason did he not bear it? Even if you are ashamed to name the cause, I will state it openly. Or rather, not I, but the truth of the facts itself. Because you killed Christ, because you stretched out your hands against the Master, because you shed the precious blood, there is no restoration for you any longer, no pardon, no defence. In those days the outrages were against servants, against Moses and Isaiah and Jeremiah. Then, even if there was some impiety, the crowning evil had not yet been dared. But now you have eclipsed all your old deeds, and through your madness against Christ you have left no excess of lawlessness unreached. That is why you are punished more severely now. For if this is not the cause of your present disgrace, why did God bear with you then, when you were killing your children, yet turns away from you now, when you dare nothing of the kind? Is it not clear that you dared something far worse and greater than child-murder and every other lawlessness, [in killing] Christ…

3. Tell me, will you still dare to call him a deceiver and a lawbreaker? Will you not go and bury yourselves somewhere, faced with so plain a truth of facts? If Jesus was a deceiver and a lawbreaker, as you say, you ought even to have won honour for killing him. Phinehas, by slaying one man, stopped the whole wrath against the nation: "Phinehas stood up," it says, "and made atonement, and the plague ceased." By the single slaughter of one lawless man he snatched so many impious people from the wrath of God. Much more ought this to have happened with you, if the one you crucified really was lawless. Why then was Phinehas justified and honoured with the priesthood for slaying a lawless man, while you, who by your own account crucified a deceiver and an enemy of God, are not only not esteemed or honoured, but have suffered worse than when you slaughtered your sons? Is it not clear even to the utterly foolish that you suffer such a penalty because you sinned against the Saviour and protector of the world? And yet now you abstain from defiling blood and keep the sabbaths, whereas then you outraged even the day itself. Through Jeremiah God promised to spare your city if you stopped carrying burdens on the sabbath. Now you do this, you do not carry burdens on the sabbath, and even so he is not reconciled to you. That sin of yours was greater than all the rest, so any reckoning of your other sins is beside the point. You are in your present calamities not because of the rest of your life, but because of that outrage. If it were not for this, God would not have turned away from you so completely, even if you had committed countless sins. This is clear both from all that has been said and from what I am about to say now. What is it? We have heard God often saying through the prophets to your fathers: "You deserved countless evils, but I act," he says, "for my name's sake, so that it may not be profaned among the nations." And again: "It is not for your sake that I act, house of Israel, but for my name's sake." What he means is this: Heavier… Five manuscripts read "will bury"; Morel reads "buried."

…[did men] take away the grace of the Spirit? Did they themselves abolish the other sacred things you had, such as the voice that came from the mercy seat, the power that attended the anointing, and the Manifestation on the priest's stones? The Jewish polity did not draw all its sources from below. Most of them, and the more sacred ones, came from above, from heaven. For example, God permitted sacrifices to be made. The altar was below, and so were the wood, the knife and the priest. But the fire that was to enter that inner sanctuary and consume the sacrifices had its origin above. No human being brought fire into the temple; a flame brought down from above performed the service of the sacrifice. Again, whenever something had to be learned, a voice came from the mercy seat between the cherubim and foretold the future. Again, on the stones on the high priest's breast, which they called the Manifestation, a flash of light would appear and signify the future. Besides this, when someone had to be anointed, the grace of the Spirit hovered over him and the oil leapt up. Prophets ministered in these matters, and a cloud and smoke often filled the inner sanctuary. So that the Jews could not be shameless or blame men for their desolation, God not only let the city fall and the temple be laid waste, but also made those things that had their origins in heaven vanish: the fire, the voice, the flashing of the stones, and all the other such things. So when a Jew says to you, "Men made war on us, men plotted against us," say to him: First of all, men would not have made war unless God allowed it. But grant that men tore down your wall. Did a man stop the fire from coming down from above? Did a man silence the voice that was continually heard from the mercy seat? Or the Manifestation on the stones? Or the priestly anointing? Did a man abolish all the rest? Was it not God who withdrew these things? That is plain to everyone. Why then did he take them away? Is it not obvious that he hated you and turned away from you once and for all? "No," he says, "we do not have these things because we do not have the mother city." And why do you not have the mother city? Is it not because God has abandoned you? Better still, to stop their shameless mouths more than sufficiently, come, let us prove this point too from the Scriptures themselves. The cause of the removal of prophecy is not the razing of the temple but the wrath of God, and the fact that they provoked him more now, through their madness against Christ, than when they worshipped the calf. When Moses prophesied, there was neither temple nor altar, and they went on committing countless impieties, yet the gift of prophecy did not fly away. On the contrary, this great and noble man himself, and seventy others besides him, were shown at that time to be prophets. And not only then. Later too, after the temple had been given along with all the rest of the worship, and then after it had been burned and everyone carried off to Babylon, Ezekiel and Daniel once again, though they did not see the holy of holies or stand beside the altar, in the middle of a land of barbarians… Another reads "nevertheless flew away." [?] Others read "and who is this about whom."

…"his life from the earth," he went on to say: "And I will give the wicked in return for his burial, and the rich in return for his death." He did not simply say "the Jews," but "the wicked." For what could be more wicked than those who, after so many benefits, [?] their benefactor? If these things have not happened, and you are not now disgraced and deprived of everything your fathers handed down; if your city has not fallen, the temple has not become a ruin, and your misfortunes have not surpassed every tragedy, then do not believe, O Jew. But if the facts cry out and the prophecy has been fulfilled, why are you shameless to no purpose and in vain? Where now are your sacred things? Where is the high priest? Where are the robe, the breastpiece and the Manifestation? Do not talk to me about these patriarchs of yours, these hucksters and traders, full of every lawlessness. Tell me, what sort of priest is there when that ancient anointing no longer exists, nor any of the rest of the sanctification? What sort of priest, tell me, when there is no sacrifice, no altar, no worship? Do you want me to tell you the laws about the priesthood, how priests were made in ancient times? Then you will learn that these men you now call patriarchs are not priests. They play at being priests and act as if on a stage. Or rather, they cannot even keep up the act. So far have they been driven away, not only from the truth but even from the pretence itself. Remember, then, how Aaron became a priest in those days: how many sacrifices Moses offered for him, how many victims he slew, how he washed him, how he anointed the lobe of his ear, his right hand and his right foot, then brought him into the holy of holies and ordered him to remain inside for a fixed number of days. But it is better to hear the very words. "This," it says, "is the anointing of Aaron and the anointing of his sons. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take Aaron and his sons, and their robes, and the oil of anointing, and the calf for the sin offering, and a ram, and assemble the congregation at the door of the tent of witness. And Moses said to all the congregation: This is the thing which the Lord commanded." When he had brought them forward (for I must abridge), he washed them with water. He put the tunic on him, girded him with the sash, clothed him with the outer robe, put on the ephod, girded him and fastened it tight. He put on the breastpiece, and on the breastpiece the Manifestation and the Truth, and the turban on his head, and on the turban the golden plate. Then he took some of the oil and sprinkled some of it on the altar and sanctified it, and the vessels, and the laver and its base, and sanctified them. He poured some of it on Aaron's head, did the same for his sons, and brought forward the calf. When Aaron and his sons had laid their hands on it and it had been slain, he took some of the blood and put it on the horns of the altar, and purified the altar. He poured out the blood at the base of the altar and sanctified it, to make atonement on it. Then, after he had burned some parts of it, some inside and some outside, he again brought a ram and [?] it whole… [?] "called." Below, [?] manuscripts read "they are able; so not." Others read "the congregation beside the door." Below, [?] manuscripts read "the congregation beside the door." Below, [?] manuscripts read "he washed him with water." Others read "brought forward."

…to await the verdict. While they were offering incense, the earth split open and swallowed all who had conspired with them, and fire from above consumed those who had taken up the censers. So that the event would not be consigned to oblivion over time, leaving later generations ignorant of God's extraordinary verdict, Moses ordered that those censers be taken and hammered into a covering around the altar. Just as the rod, though it had no voice, gave forth a voice through its appearance, so these plates too were to speak to everyone who came after. They were to exhort and advise them never to imitate the folly of those before them, so that they would not suffer the same punishment. Do you see how priests were ordained in ancient times? But now everything among the Jews is a farce, a laughingstock and a disgrace, huckstering full of countless lawless deeds. Tell me, do you follow these people, who are always bent on doing and saying everything contrary to God's laws, and do you run to their synagogues? Are you not afraid that a thunderbolt may come down from above and burn up your head? Do you not know that even someone who is not a robber, if he is seen in the robbers' den, pays the same penalty as they do? And why do I speak of robbers? Surely you all know and remember the time when some defiled men and sorcerers pulled down the statues here among us. Not only those who dared the deed, but everyone who was simply seen present at what happened, was hauled off to court, led away with them, and paid the ultimate penalty. Yet you, tell me, hurry to run where the Father is insulted, the Son blasphemed, and the holy and life-giving Spirit rejected? Are you not afraid, do you not shudder, bringing yourself into those profane and unclean places? Tell me, what defence will you have, what pardon, when you willingly push yourself into the pit and throw yourself down the cliffs? Do not tell me that the law and the books of the prophets are kept there. That is not enough to make a place holy. Which is greater: that books lie in a place, or that someone speaks the words from those books? Clearly, speaking the words from the books and holding them in one's mind. What then, tell me? When the devil spoke from the Scriptures, was his mouth sanctified? You cannot say so. He remained the devil. And what of the demons? They proclaimed, "These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation." Shall we therefore rank them among the apostles? By no means. We still turn away from them and hate them just the same. So do words spoken aloud fail to sanctify, while books lying there do? How could that make sense? This above all is why I hate the synagogue: because it has the law and the prophets. I hate it more now than if it had none of these. Why? Because it is a great bait, and from it comes great deception for simpler people. That was also why Paul drove out that demon: because it spoke instead of keeping silent. "Being greatly troubled in spirit," it says, "he said, 'Come out of her.'" And why? Because it cried out, "These men are servants of the Most High God." While they kept silent they did not deceive so much, but by speaking they were going to drag along many of the simpler people and… Six manuscripts and Savile [?] (thus [?]: "is consigned, and ignorance"). [?] reads "prepare" instead of "make"; after "verdict" [?].

Back then, when the cherubim were there, when the ark was there, when the grace of the Spirit still flourished, he said at one point, "You have made it a den of robbers," and at another, "a house of trade," because of their lawlessness and their murders. Now that the grace of the Spirit has abandoned them, and all those sacred things have been taken away, and they carry out this unlawful worship out of contentiousness [?], what name could anyone give their synagogues and find a fitting one? If it was a den of robbers back then, when their way of life still held sway, then now, whether you call it a brothel, a place of lawlessness, a lodging of demons, a fortress of the devil, the ruin of souls, a cliff and a pit of every kind of destruction, whatever you call it, you will be saying less than it deserves. Do you want to see a temple? Do not run to the synagogue; become a temple yourself. God destroyed one temple in Jerusalem, and raised up countless others far more sacred than that one. "For you are the temple of the living God," he says. Adorn this house. Drive out every evil thought, so that you may become a precious member of Christ and a temple of the Spirit, and make others like this too. You would not easily walk past the poor when you see them. In the same way, when you see someone running to the synagogue, do not walk past him. Hold him back with your words as if with a bridle, and lead him back to the Church. This is a greater act of charity than that one, and its reward is greater than ten thousand talents. And [?] [Editorial note:] Others read "sacred things, contending against God," notes Montfaucon, who [?] reads "sacred and dear to God, the u[nlawful] …" "… but with as much zeal and eagerness." [?]

AGAINST THE JEWS. Seventh Discourse. Have you had your fill [?] of the battle against the Jews, or do you want us to take up the same subject again today? Although a great deal was said before, I still think you want to hear about it again. Whoever never has his fill of love for Christ will never have his fill of battle against those who hate him. Besides, this discourse is necessary for us in any case, since traces of their festivals still remain. Their trumpets were more lawless than the trumpets in the theaters, and their fasts more shameful than drunkenness and every kind of revelry. In the same way, the tabernacles they are now putting up are no better than inns that keep prostitutes and flute-girls. Let no one condemn my words as audacious. It would be the height of audacity and lawlessness not to hold such suspicions about them. When they act in contention with God and in opposition to the Holy Spirit, how can we not pass such a verdict on them? This feast was sacred once, when it was held according to the law and at God's command, but it is no longer. Its whole dignity has been taken away, because it is held against God's will. The people who most outrage both the law and the ancient feasts are the very ones who now seem to be celebrating them, while we, who most honor the law, are like people letting an old man rest, and

… they read the law outside [?], and made confession. If, then, it was not even possible for the law to be read outside the city, how could it be practiced outside the city? This is why he threatened them, saying, "I will not punish your daughters when they play the harlot, nor your brides when they commit adultery." What does this mean? I will read you an ancient law and try to make it clearer. What, then, is the law? "If a woman goes astray from her husband and disregards him in contempt, and a man lies with her carnally, and it is hidden from her husband's eyes, and there is no witness against her, and she has not been caught, and a spirit of jealousy comes upon him, though she has not been defiled." What he means is this: if a woman commits adultery, he says, and her husband suspects adultery, or if she has not committed adultery but he suspects it, and there is neither a witness nor a pregnancy to convict her, he shall bring her to the priest, he says, and offer her offering of barley meal. Why not fine flour, why not wheat meal, but barley? Because what was taking place was mourning, condemnation and evil suspicion, the form of the sacrifice imitated the misfortune [?] that belonged to it. That is why he says, "You shall not pour oil on it, nor put frankincense on it." Then (for I must abridge) "the priest shall bring her forward and take pure water in an earthen vessel, and take some of the dust on the floor and throw it into the water. He shall set the woman in place, put her under oath, and say: 'If you have not gone astray to be defiled against your own husband, be unharmed by this water of conviction. But if you have gone astray and been defiled, and some man other than your husband has lain with you, may the Lord make you a curse and an oath in the midst of the people.'" What does "a curse and an oath" mean? It means that people will say, "May I not suffer what that woman suffered." "'When the Lord makes your belly burst, the accursed water shall enter to burst your womb.' And the woman shall say, 'So be it, so be it.' And if she has been defiled, the water of conviction shall enter and burst her belly, and the woman shall become a curse. But if the woman has not been defiled, she shall be innocent and shall conceive seed." So once they had gone into captivity, none of this could take place: there was no temple, no altar, no tabernacle, and no sacrifice being offered. That is why he threatened them, saying, "I will not punish your daughters when they play the harlot, nor your brides when they commit adultery." 2. Do you see that the law has its force from the place? And this makes it clear that there cannot be a priest when there is no city. There cannot be a king without armies, without a diadem, without the purple, without the other things that make up kingship. In the same way, there cannot be a priest when sacrifice has been abolished, offering prevented, the holy things trampled underfoot and the whole order wiped out, for the priesthood consisted in all of these. What I said a moment ago would indeed be enough to prove to us that neither sacrifices, nor burnt offerings, nor the other purifications, nor anything else of the … [Editorial note:] Others read "he would pour" or "he will put." Manuscripts: "and he sank [?] sins."

… destroyed sins, quenched death, opened the heavens, showed us many great hopes and arranged everything else. Paul knew this too, and cried out, "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!" Foreseeing all these things, then, he said, "Many, O Lord my God, are the wonders you have done." Then, having said in the person of Christ, "In burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure," he added, "Then I said, Behold, I come." Then: when? When the time has come for the more perfect teachings. The less perfect things had to be learned through his servants, but the loftier things that go beyond human nature had to be learned from the Lawgiver himself. That is why Paul said, "In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old to our fathers by the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages." And again John says, "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." So this too is the greatest praise of the law: it prepared human nature for the Teacher. Then, so that you would not think he was a new God, or that he was bringing in some innovation, hear what he says: "In the scroll of the book it is written of me." Long ago, he says, the prophets foretold my coming, and at the beginning of the books they opened up to people the knowledge of my divinity. 3. So when God says at the beginning of creation, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," he is revealing to us in a riddle the divinity of the Son, to whom he is speaking. Then he shows that this is not contrary to the earlier way of life, but that this too was God's will: that the earlier sacrifice should be abolished and this one brought in to replace it. (It was an intensifying of the correction, not opposition or conflict.) So, having said, "In the scroll of the book it is written of me," he added, "I desired to do your will, O God, and your law is in the midst of my belly." Then, when he says what God's will is, he passes over sacrifice, burnt offerings, offerings, toil and sweat, and says, "I proclaimed the good news of righteousness in the great congregation." What does "I proclaimed the good news of righteousness" mean? He did not simply say "I gave," but "I proclaimed the good news." Why? Because he justified our race not by good deeds, nor by labors, nor by [?], but by grace alone. Paul made this clear too when he said, "But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been manifested, the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ," not through some toil and labor. And he took up this very testimony and said: "For since the law has a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the realities, it can never perfect those who draw near by the same sacrifices that they offer continually, year after year. Therefore, when he comes into the world, he says: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire," [Editorial note:] Five manuscripts: "for sin you did not seek"; others: "you did not [?] … of necessary things." Six manuscripts: "I opened up." [?] Shortly after, the same read "have been brought in."

… full of blood. This is not an accusation against the sacrifices but a charge against the wickedness of those who offered them. He would not accept the sacrifices because they offered them with defiled hands. Again David, after saying, "I will not accept bulls from your house, nor goats from your flocks," went on: "But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant in your mouth? You hated discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran along with him, and you threw in your lot with adulterers. Your mouth multiplied wickedness, and your tongue wove deceits. You sat and spoke against your brother, and laid a stumbling block before your mother's son." From this it is clear that he did not reject the sacrifices here without qualification, but because they committed adultery, because they stole, because they plotted against their brothers. And each of the prophets, they say, accuses those who offer the sacrifices, and so says that God rejects them in this sense. 4. This is what our opponents say to us. But Paul has dealt them a sufficient blow and fully stopped the mouth of their shamelessness with this testimony. He wanted to show that God rejected that way of life itself as imperfect and made it inoperative, so he took up this testimony, which contains no accusation against those who offered sacrifice, and in which its imperfection is laid bare on its own. The prophet accuses the Jews of nothing. He simply says, "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure." And interpreting this, Paul said, "He abolishes the first in order to establish the second." If he had said, "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire," and then fallen silent, the argument would have left some room for a defense. But as it is, by saying, "But a body you prepared for me," and showing that another sacrifice had been brought in, he left no further hope that the first would return. And interpreting this very point, Paul said, "Through this offering we have been sanctified by the will of Christ." "For if the blood of bulls and goats," he says, "and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are defiled sanctify for the purity of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish, cleanse our conscience from dead works?" This is enough to show that those things have ceased, that others have been brought in to replace them, and that the old will not be restored. Come, then. We have long been eager to show that the old form of priesthood also no longer exists and will never return. Let us make this plain, expressly and clearly, from their own Scriptures. But first let me tell you a few things, so that the interpretation of what is said may be clearer. When Abraham came back from Persia, he fathered Isaac; Isaac fathered Jacob; Jacob fathered the twelve patriarchs, from whom came twelve tribes, or rather thirteen; [Editorial note:] [?] "Since you desired; then, having said [?] you desired, the argument would have had some room for a defense; but now, by saying, But a body you prepared."

5. Then, so that no one would suspect this was said about some ordinary man, it is not Isaiah who says it, nor Jeremiah, nor any other prophet who was a private person, but the king himself, [so that you may learn that] a king can call no one his Lord except God alone. If he had been a private person, perhaps one of the shameless would have said that he was speaking about a man. But as it is, being a king, he would not have called a man his Lord. And if David were saying these things about some ordinary man, how could he have said that he sat at the right hand of that ineffable and great glory? That is impossible. But it is about him that he says, "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." Then, so that you would not think him weak and powerless, he added, "With you is dominion in the day of your power." And to show it more clearly he said, "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you." But no human being has been born before the morning star. "You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." He did not say "according to the order of Aaron." So ask the Jew: if the old priesthood was not going to be abolished, why did he bring in another priest according to the order of Melchizedek? See how Paul made this very passage clearer when he came to it. Having said of Christ, "as he says in another place, You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek," he added, "About him we have much to say, and it is hard to explain." Then, after rebuking the disciples (for I must abridge), he explains who Melchizedek is and brings in the story, saying, "This is the one who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and to whom Abraham also apportioned a tenth of everything." Then, unveiling the meaning of the type, he says, "See how great this man is, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of everything." He did not say this idly. He wanted to show that our priesthood is far greater than the Jewish one, and that its superiority was shown in advance in the very types of the realities. Abraham was the father of Isaac, the grandfather of Jacob, and the ancestor of Levi, for Levi was Jacob's son, and the priesthood among the Jews began with Levi. Yet this Abraham, the ancestor of the Levites and of the Jewish priests, held the rank of a layman in relation to Melchizedek, who was a type of our priesthood. He showed this in two ways: by giving him a tenth, since laymen give tithes to priests, and by being blessed by him, since laymen are blessed by priests. See again how great the superiority of our priesthood is, when Abraham, the patriarch of the Jews and ancestor of the Levites, is found being blessed by Melchizedek and giving him tithes. The Old Testament says both things: that Melchizedek blessed Abraham, and that he received tithes from him. Paul brought forward these very facts and said, "See how great this man is." Who is this man? Melchizedek, he says, to whom Abraham, their patriarch, gave a tenth of the spoils. "And those of the sons of Levi …" [?] Abraham, and that he received tithes from him. These things, then [?].

… For [it is evident] that our Lord has sprung from Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priesthood. Christ is shown to be from that tribe, that is, Judah, and a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and Melchizedek is far more venerable than Abraham. So it is agreed on every side that one priesthood is being brought in to replace another, and that it is far loftier than the first. If the type was like this, and more splendid than the Jewish priesthood, the truth itself is much more so. To establish this, he said, "And it is still more evident if another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life." What does "not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life" mean? That none of his commandments was fleshly. He did not command us to sacrifice sheep and calves, but to serve God through virtue of the soul, and as the prize for these he set before us a life that never comes to an end. And again, when we had been made dead by our sins, he came and raised us up and made us alive, [destroying (?)] a double death: one of sin, the other of the flesh. Since he came bringing us such good things, he says, "not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life." 5 [?]. This too has now been demonstrated along the way: once the priesthood was changed, a change of law also had to follow of necessity. Still, it would have been possible to demonstrate this expressly as well, and to bring forward the prophets again as witnesses saying that the law will be changed, that the way of life will be transformed for the better, and that no Jewish king will ever rise again. But one must say only as much as the hearer can take in, not everything at once or all together. So we will store those points up for another occasion and end the discourse here for now. I urge you, beloved, to remember what has been said and to join it to what was said before. And what I asked of you before, I will ask now too: rescue your brothers, and take great care of the members who have been neglected. This is why we take on such labor: not just to speak, nor to enjoy applause and acclaim, but to lead those who have broken away back to the way of truth. Let no one say to me, "I have nothing to do with him. If only I can set my own affairs right." No one can set his own affairs right without love for his neighbor and care for his salvation. That is why Paul says, "Let no one seek his own good, but each the good of the other," knowing that a person's own good lies in his neighbor's benefit. Are you healthy, while your brother is sick? If you are right-minded, you will grieve all the more for the one who is suffering, and in this too you will imitate that blessed man who says, "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" For if, by laying out two obols and spending a little [?] [Editorial note:] [?] "and the prizes of these." Morel and Savile: "prizes." [?] "the way of life [?] transformed."

…those who have been taken captive by him to do his will. And let us not give up until we have done everything on our part, whether they are persuaded or not. Or rather, it is impossible for people who are Christians not to be persuaded. But so that you may not have even this excuse, I say this: when you have spent many words and done everything you can, and you see that he is still not persuaded, bring him to the priests. By the grace of God they will surely capture their quarry, and the whole credit will be yours, since you led him by the hand. Husbands, talk about these things with your wives; wives, with your husbands; fathers, with your children; friends, with your friends. Let the Jews learn them too, and so should those who seem to be ranked with us but [keep] their…

AGAINST THE JEWS. Eighth Discourse. 1. The fast of the Jews has passed, or rather the drunkenness of the Jews. For it is possible to be drunk even without wine. It is possible to behave like a drunkard while sober, and to revel in debauchery. If it were not possible to be drunk without wine, the prophet would not have said, "Woe to those who are drunk, but not from wine." If it were not possible to be drunk without wine, Paul would not have said, "Do not get drunk with wine." He said "Do not get drunk with wine" because one can also be drunk in other ways. Yes, one can be drunk with anger, with unnatural desire, with love of money, with vainglory, and with countless other passions. For drunkenness is nothing other than a departure from right reasoning, a derangement, the destruction of the soul's health. So it is not only the man who pours down a great deal of unmixed wine who can rightly be called drunk, but also the man who nourishes some other passion in his soul. The man who lusts after a woman not his own, and spends his time with prostitutes, is drunk. The man who has drunk much unmixed wine loses control of himself, utters slavish words and sees one thing in place of another. In the same way this man, filled with this licentious desire as if with unmixed wine, utters no sound word. Everything he says is shameful, corrupt, slavish and laughable. He too sees one thing in place of another. He is blind to what is in front of him, yet everywhere he pictures the woman he longs to outrage. Like someone out of his mind and raving, in meetings, at banquets, at every time and in every place, though countless people say countless things to him, he does not seem to hear. He is wholly bent on her, and he dreams of the sin. He suspects and fears everything, no better off than an animal caught in the hunter's net. The man gripped by anger is drunk as well. His face swells, his voice grows harsh, his eyes become bloodshot, his mind is darkened, his understanding is drowned, his tongue trembles, his eyes roll, and his ears hear one thing in place of another. His anger strikes his brain harder than any unmixed wine, stirring up a storm and an inconsolable tempest. But if a man gripped by desire or anger is drunk, much more so is an impious man who blasphemes God… (Mss.: "might fittingly." Another reading: "his tongue stumbles.") …let us do. For they, when… [?]

…to return to its own life and to recognize its Master. 2. But let us not grow weary, brothers. Let us not lose heart or fall back. And let no one say those words to me: "We should have made things safe before the fast and done everything then. But now, after the fasting, after the sin has been committed, after the lawlessness has been carried out, what good is it any more?" Anyone who knows what it means to care for one's brothers also knows that now above all we must set to work and show all our zeal. We must not only provide safeguards before the sin; we must also stretch out a hand after the fall. If God had acted that way from the beginning, safeguarding us only before the sin, then giving up on us after it and leaving us to lie forever where we fell, not one of us would ever have been saved. But he does not do this. He loves humankind, he is gentle, and he longs above all for our salvation, so even after our sins he shows great care for us. He did indeed safeguard Adam before the sin, and said to him: "You may eat freely of every tree in the garden, but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. On the day you eat of it, you shall surely die." See how he safeguarded man in every way that he ought to have been safeguarded: by the ease of the law, by the abundance of what was permitted, by the penalty of the coming punishment, and by how swiftly it would fall. He did not say after one, two or three days, but on that very day: "On the day you eat of it, you shall surely die." Yet after all that care and teaching and warning and kindness Adam fell, and he did not listen to the commands. Even so, God did not say, "What more is there to do? What good is it? He ate, he fell, he broke the law, he trusted the devil, he dishonored my commandment, he took the wound, he became a dead man, he was handed over to death, he came under sentence. Why should I speak to him any more?" He said none of this. Instead he came to him at once, spoke with him and comforted him. He also applied another remedy, that of toil and sweat. And he did not stop doing and contriving everything until he had raised up the fallen nature, freed it from death and led it by the hand to heaven. He gave greater goods than those that had been lost, and by these very deeds he taught the devil that he had gained nothing by his plot. The devil drove human beings out of paradise, but a little later he will see them in heaven, mingling with the angels. God did the same with Cain. He safeguarded him too before the sin and warned him in advance, saying, "You have sinned; be still. His turning shall be toward you, and you shall rule over him." See his wisdom and understanding. "Are you afraid," he says, "that because of the honor I have given him he will take from you the precedence of the firstborn, and seize the rule that belongs to you? For the firstborn had to be held in greater honor than the second-born. Take courage," he says, "do not be afraid or anxious about this. His turning shall be toward you, and you…" (Some mss.: "it was needful"; and below: "to safeguard." Others: "he presented himself to all who met him.")

…[thinking himself] worthy of no defense, could he not wash away his sins (even though the prophet says, "Tell your iniquities first, so that you may be justified")? Why was he even condemned? Because he did not tell them as the prophet commanded. The prophet did not simply say, "Tell your iniquities." What did he say? "Tell your iniquities first." That is what is required: not simply to tell them, but to tell them first, and not wait for someone to convict and accuse you. Cain did not tell first. He waited to be convicted by God; or rather, he denied it even while God was convicting him. Only when God had plainly exposed what had happened did he speak of his sin, and that is no longer confession. So you too, beloved, when you sin, do not wait for someone else to accuse you. Before you are accused and denounced, condemn what you have done yourself. If someone else convicts you, the merit no longer belongs to your confession; the correction comes from his accusation. That is why another writer says, "The righteous man accuses himself in the first words he speaks." So what is required is not simply to accuse oneself, but to accuse oneself first, and not to wait for others to convict. Peter, for example, after that grievous denial, quickly called his sin to mind. With no one accusing him, he spoke of his offense and wept bitterly. In this way he washed away that denial so completely that he became the first of the apostles and was entrusted with the whole world. But as I was saying (I must return to my subject), the argument has shown us clearly enough from this that when our brothers fall we must not neglect or despise them. We must safeguard them before the sin, and after the sin we must show them great care. Doctors do the same. They tell people what can preserve their health and ward off every disease even while they are well. But when people neglect the instructions and fall ill, the doctors do not abandon them. It is then above all that they show the greatest care, so as to free them from their diseases. Paul acted the same way. After the fornicator's sin, that grievous lawlessness not found even among the Gentiles, Paul did not abandon him. The man resisted. He refused to accept the treatment, kicking and leaping away, yet Paul brought him back to be healed, and brought him back so fully as to unite him once more with the body of the Church. He did not say to himself, "What more is there to do? What good is it? He has committed fornication and done the sin. He does not even want to give up his licentiousness; he is puffed up and proud, and is making the wound incurable. Let us leave him, then, and abandon him." He said none of this. On the contrary, it was for this very reason that he showed such great care then, because he saw that the man had slipped into unspeakable wickedness. He did not stop frightening him, threatening him and punishing him, both by himself and through many others, doing and contriving everything, until he brought him to recognize his sin and become aware of his transgression, and freed him completely from every stain. This… (Five mss.: "with no one accusing, he recognized the…" …to snatch away [?]. Edd.)

…this will make you more [?]. For "whoever brings forth the precious from the worthless," he says, "shall be as my mouth." What could equal this? Neither fasting, nor sleeping on the ground, nor all-night vigils, nor anything else can achieve what the salvation of a brother achieves. Think how often your mouth has sinned, how many shameful words it has spoken, how many blasphemies and insults it has hurled. Then you will surely take up the care of the fallen, for through this one good deed you will be able to wash away all that stain. Why do I say wash away? You will make your mouth the mouth of God. What honor could equal this? Am I the one making these promises? God himself said it: "If you bring forth even one," he says, "your mouth shall be as my mouth," pure and holy. So let us not neglect our brothers, or go about saying, "How many fasted? How many were swept away?" Let us take care of them instead. Even if many have fasted, beloved, do not parade it, and do not make a public spectacle of the Church's misfortune. Heal it. If someone says, "Many fasted," stop his mouth, so that the report does not spread, and say to him: "I know of no one. You have been deceived, man, and you are lying. If you see two or three swept away, you say there are many." Stop the mouth of the accuser, and do not neglect those who have been swept away. Then the Church will be made secure on both sides: the report will not be paraded about, and those who were swept away will be led back to the holy flock. So let us not go about saying, "Who has sinned?" Let us strive only to correct those who have sinned. It is a terrible habit, truly terrible, only to accuse our brothers and not to care for them, to parade the faults of the weak and not to heal them. Let us get rid of this wicked habit, then, beloved, for it does no small harm. I will tell you how. Someone heard you say that many had fasted with the Jews. Without checking anything, he carried the word to another. That man in turn, without asking any questions, told it to someone else. Then, as this wicked report grows little by little, great reproach is spread over the Church. The lost gain nothing from it; instead, harm is done both to them and to many others. Even if they are few, we make them many by spreading the report widely. We make those who are standing weaker, and we push those who are about to fall. A brother who hears that many fasted will himself grow more careless, and the weak man who hears it will run to join the crowd of the fallen. So let us take no pleasure in this or in any other wickedness, even if many are sinning, so as to parade them and say, "There are many." Let us stop mouths and hold them in check. Do not tell me that many fasted; correct the many. I did not spend so many words so that you could accuse the many, but so that you could make the many few, or rather not even few, so that you could save them too. So do not parade… (…is spread over [?]. Some mss.: "by these reports" (Savile: "evil") "many." …even if those who sin are many, not to parade [?]…)

…of the [?], the [refutation] from the temple and from the predictions of the prophets. Show how they do everything rashly and in vain, that they will never return to their former way of life, and that they are not permitted to perform any such rite outside Jerusalem. Besides this, remind him of Gehenna, of the fearful judgment seat of the Lord, and of the reckoning there. Remind him that we shall give an account of all these things, and that no small punishment awaits those who dare such things. Remind him too of Paul, who says, "You who would be justified by the law have fallen away from grace," and who warns again, "If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you." Tell him that Jewish fasting, like circumcision, shuts the one who fasts out of heaven, even if he has countless other good deeds to his credit. Tell him that we are called Christians, and are Christians, so that we may obey Christ, not so that we may run to those enemies. And if he pleads some cure and says to you, "They promise to heal me, and that is why I run to them," expose their trickery, their incantations, their amulets and their sorceries. That is the only way they seem to heal; they do not truly heal, God forbid! But I will go much further and say this: even if they truly healed, it would be better to die than to run to the enemies of God and be healed in this way. What good is it for the body to be healed while the soul perishes? What gain is there in finding some comfort here if we are to be sent off into the undying fire? So that they cannot say these things, listen to what Moses says: "If a prophet arises among you, or one who dreams a dream, and gives a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder he spoke of comes to pass, and he says, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' you shall not listen to that prophet, for the Lord your God is testing you, to see whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul." What he means is this. Suppose some prophet says, "I can raise a dead man or heal a blind man, but listen to me and let us worship the demons," or "let us practice idolatry." Then suppose the man who says this is able to heal the blind man or raise the dead. Do not be persuaded even then, he says. Why? Because God, testing you [?], allowed him to be able to do this. It was not that God did not know your mind, but he wished to give you a test of whether you truly love God. For it is the mark of one who loves not to betray any part [?], and not to turn away even if those who strive to drag us from the one we love show us the dead rising. If he said this to the Jews, much more does it apply to us. He has led us to a higher wisdom. He has opened the door of the resurrection to us. He commands us not to linger over present things, but to place all our hopes in the life to come. What pardon, then, will we have, when those people suffered and endured so much, while we, for a fever or for wounds, run to the synagogues and call sorcerers and enchanters into our own homes? Have you not heard what Scripture says? "My child, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for testing. Set your heart straight and endure… in sickness and poverty, trusting in him. For gold is tested in the fire, and acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation." 6. But what do you say? That the sickness of your body afflicts and oppresses you? You have not yet suffered as much as blessed Job, or rather not even the smallest part of what he suffered. After the sudden loss of his flocks and herds and everything else, the whole company of his children was also snatched away. And all this happened in a single day, so that not only the nature of the trials but also their quick succession might overthrow the athlete. After all that, [he received] a deadly [blow] in his body… If you whip your own servant, and after taking thirty or fifty strokes he immediately cries out for his freedom, or leaves your household and goes off to some people who hate you and provokes you, tell me, will he be able to obtain pardon? Will anyone be able to speak in his defense? Not at all. Why? Because it is proper for a master… (…of the wife. …for them nothing outside Jerusalem. …Savile: "of those.")
…to punish a servant. And not only for this reason, but also because, if he had to flee for refuge, he should not have fled to the enemies or to those who hate [his master], but to his true friends…

7. So you too, when you see God punishing you, do not flee to his enemies the Jews, or you will provoke him all the more. Flee to his friends instead: the martyrs, the saints, those who have pleased him and have great boldness before him. But why do I speak of servants and masters? [A son] cannot do this because his father whips him, nor can he deny that he is his father's kin. The laws of nature and the laws laid down by human beings alike command him to bear everything nobly, even if his father whips him, keeps him from the table, throws him out of the house, or punishes him in any other way. If he does not obey and will not endure it, no one grants him any pardon. However much the boy may wail after being whipped, everyone says the same words to him: "It was your father who whipped you. He is your lord, he has authority to do whatever he likes, and you must bear it all meekly." Servants, then, put up with their masters, and sons with their fathers, often even when they are punished undeservedly. Will you not put up with God disciplining you? He has more authority than any master. He loves you more than any father. He does nothing out of anger, but contrives and does everything for your good. Yet if some small illness comes, you immediately leap out from under his lordship, run to the demons, and desert to the synagogues? What pardon will you obtain after that? How will you be able to entreat him again? Or rather, who else will be able to pray for you, even if he has the boldness of Moses? There is no one. Do you not hear what God says to Jeremiah about the Jews? "Do not pray for this people, for even if Moses and Samuel were to stand before me, I would not listen to them." So there are some sins that are beyond all pardon and admit no defense. Let us not, then, draw such wrath upon ourselves. For even if they seem to relieve the fever with their incantations (and they do not relieve it), they bring another, more grievous fever into the conscience. Your reason stings you every day, and your conscience whips you and says: "You have been impious, you have broken the law, you have violated your covenant with Christ. For a little illness you betrayed your faith. Are you the only one who has suffered these things? Have not others suffered far worse than you? Yet none of them dared to do anything like this. But you, slack and weak-willed, have sacrificed your own soul. How will you defend yourself before Christ? How will you call upon him in your prayers? With what conscience will you set foot in the church after this? With what eyes will you look at the priest? With what hand will you touch the holy table? With what ears will you hear the Scriptures read there?" Your reason will say these things to you, stinging you every day, and your conscience will whip you. What sort of health is this, when we have such accusers within us? But if you endure a little while, and those who wish either… (So [?] mss. Montfaucon: "or rather, no one else," which is less [?]. Some mss.: "whipping. What fever will it not surpass? What then…")

…once seized by it [the fever], when countless people urged him to get rid of the disease, he, for the sake of my name and out of fear of me, so as not to offend in anything, drove away and dishonored those who promised to heal him in that way, and chose rather to die of the disease than to betray his loyalty to me.” For if he brings forward those who gave him drink, clothed him and fed him, how much more will he bring forward those who chose to endure fevers for his sake! Giving bread and a cloak is not the same as enduring a long illness; the second is far greater than the first. And the greater the toil, the more splendid the crown will be. Let us reflect on these things both in health and in sickness, and let us tell them to others. And if we ever find ourselves in an unbearable fever, let us say this to ourselves: “What if some accusation had been brought against us, and we had been hauled into court, and then strung up and had our sides torn with hooks? Would we not have had to endure it all the same, without gain and without any reward?” Let us think about this now as well. So let the reward of patience also be added, which is enough to strengthen the fallen mind. “But the fever is hard.” Then set against the fever the fire of Gehenna, which you will surely escape if you choose to bear this fever with all patience. Remember the apostles and how much they suffered. Remember the righteous, and how they were constantly in afflictions. Remember blessed Timothy, how he never had relief from his illness but lived with constant sickness. Paul made this plain when he said, “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.” If that righteous and holy man, who had been entrusted with the care of the whole world, who raised the dead, drove out demons and cured countless diseases in others, suffered such hardships, what defense will you have, you who are troubled and fret over passing illnesses? Have you not heard Scripture say, “Whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives”? How many people, how many times, have longed to receive the crown of martyrdom? This is a complete crown of martyrdom. For it is not only being ordered to sacrifice, and then choosing to die rather than sacrifice, that makes a martyr. Keeping any commandment at all, when doing so can bring death on oneself, is also martyrdom…

8. To learn that this is true, remember how John died, and for what cause and why, and how Abel died. Neither of them saw an altar burning or an idol standing, and neither was ordered to sacrifice to demons. John was beheaded simply because he rebuked Herod. Abel was slaughtered because he honored God with a greater sacrifice than his brother did. Were they then deprived of the crowns of martyrdom? Who would dare to say so? Above all, the manner of their death is itself enough to convince everyone that they rank among the foremost of the martyrs. And if you want to see a divine verdict pronounced on their behalf, listen to what Paul says. Whatever he utters clearly belongs to the Spirit, for he says, “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” What then [?]? And do not be surprised [?], for if… [Notes:] b Montfaucon [?]: “let it be set before patience too.” But seven manuscripts read as we do. [?] Others: “are laws of the Spirit. I think.”

…but with God watching, who is present everywhere, do you shamelessly dare to commit this lawless act? Do you not fear God? Then at least feel shame before the Jews themselves. With what eyes will you look at them, and with what mouth will you speak to them, when you confess that you are a Christian yet run to their synagogues and beg for their help? Do you not realize how much they laugh at you, how much they mock and jeer at you, how much shame and disgrace they heap on you, if not openly, then in their own minds? 9. So tell me, is this bearable or tolerable? Even if you had to die ten thousand deaths, even if you had to suffer incurable torments, would it not be far better to endure every hardship than to become a laughingstock and an object of mockery to those vile people, and to live with an evil conscience? I say this not only so that you may hear it, but so that you may cure those who are sick in this way. For just as we reproach them for being weak in faith, so we reproach you for not wanting to set the weak right. Is this all that is required, beloved: that you come in here and hear what is said? Rather, that itself brings judgment, when action does not follow the hearing of the words. Are you not a Christian so that you may imitate Christ and obey his laws? And what did he do? He did not sit in Jerusalem and summon the sick to himself. He went around cities and villages, healing both kinds of sickness, that of the body and that of the soul. Yet he could have sat in one place and drawn everyone to himself. He did not do this, and so gave us an example of going around and seeking those who are perishing. He hinted at the same thing again in the parable of the shepherd. For he did not sit with the ninety-nine sheep and wait for the stray one to come to him. He went off himself and found it, and when he had found it he carried it on his shoulders and brought it back. Do you not see that physicians do exactly this? They do not make the sick, lying on their beds, be carried to their houses; they run to the sick themselves. Do this too, beloved, knowing that the present life is short, and that if we do not make these gains we shall have no salvation there. Often a single soul that has been won can wipe out a mass of countless sins and become a ransom for us on that day. Consider why prophets, why apostles, why righteous men, why angels were sent so many times, and why the only-begotten Son of God himself came. Was it not to save human beings? Was it not so that those who had gone astray… [Notes:] f [?] “but running to the […] and the […]” [?]. Next, Morel has “or that vile man,” but [?] and most of the manuscripts have “or those vile people.” [?] of [Chry]sostom, in six discourses. But one has “in five discourses.”

…read as follows: “But what do those say who are terrible in every kind of wickedness? ‘That man,’ he says, ‘has become a heretic, with the devil dwelling in him, speaking unrighteousness against God, and by persuasive talk and empty deceit leading many into the abyss of perdition. For this reason he has been expelled by the fathers, especially since his teacher cut off a portion of the Church,’” meaning either [?] (read Paulinus) or Apollinarius. That is, but…
